claim: NG2 cells are a large population of self-renewing cells present in substantial numbers in all white and grey matter regions of the CNS throughout development and adulthood
source: NG2-expressing glial cells (NG2 cells) are a large population of self-renewing cells present in substantial numbers in all white and grey matter regions of the CNS throughout development and adulthood (Nishiyama et al., 1999; Butt et al., 2005; Trotter et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Nishiyama et al., 1999; Butt et al., 2005; Trotter et al., 2010).

claim: NG2 cells are precursor cells to all oligodendrocytes
source: NG2 cells are precursor cells to all oligodendrocytes, which exclusively provide isolating myelin to axons and are thereby essential for rapid conduction velocity while maintaining small axon diameter in compact brains.
evidence: This claim is stated as established knowledge in the field without specific citations in this sentence, drawing from general scientific consensus.

claim: Oligodendrocytes exclusively provide isolating myelin to axons
source: NG2 cells are precursor cells to all oligodendrocytes, which exclusively provide isolating myelin to axons and are thereby essential for rapid conduction velocity while maintaining small axon diameter in compact brains.
evidence: This claim is stated as established knowledge about oligodendrocyte function.

claim: Myelination is plastic and activity-dependent
source: Recent evidence suggests that myelination is plastic and activity-dependent and that synaptic transmission to NG2 cells plays a key role in detecting patterns of activity.
evidence: This claim is presented as recent evidence from the field, though specific citations are not provided in this sentence.

claim: NG2 cells receive direct vesicular synaptic input from neighboring axons
source: NG2 cells stand out from other glial cells as they receive direct vesicular synaptic input from neighboring axons (Bergles et al., 2000; Lin and Bergles, 2004; Jabs et al., 2005; Ge et al., 2006; Kukley et al., 2007; Ziskin et al., 2007; Karadottir et al., 2008; Kukley et al., 2008; Velez-Fort et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Release of neurotransmitter onto NG2 cells may be the key signal mediating activity-dependent myelination
source: based on these findings, it has recently been proposed that release of neurotransmitter onto NG2 cells may be the key signal mediating activity-dependent myelination and instructing the cells about the need to generate more oligodendrocytes and myelin (Wake et al., 2011; Hines et al., 2015; Mensch et al., 2015; Koudelka et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent publications proposing this mechanism.

claim: NG2 cells express a large number of voltage-gated ion channels
source: NG2 cells are also unique amongst glial cells as they express a large number of voltage-gated ion channels (VGCs) (Chittajallu et al., 2004; Jabs et al., 2005; Karadottir et al., 2008; De Biase et al., 2010; Kukley et al., 2010; Clarke et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: NG2 cells are not capable of firing action potentials
source: NG2 cells are not capable of firing action potentials (Bergles et al., 2000; Lin et al., 2005; Tong et al., 2009; De Biase et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: Postsynaptic potentials in NG2 cells are very small
source: their postsynaptic potentials (PSPs) are so small (Jabs et al., 2005; Haberlandt et al., 2011) that it has been questioned whether synaptic input can even achieve a relevant depolarization to recruit VGCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two published studies.

claim: Previous attempts to elicit calcium signals in NG2 cells by synaptic stimulation failed
source: Furthermore, previous attempts to elicit calcium signals in NG2 cells by synaptic stimulation failed and led the authors to conclude that the synaptic input was too weak (Velez-Fort et al., 2010; Haberlandt et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two published studies that reported failed attempts.

claim: The density of synapses on NG2 cells might be massively underestimated
source: On the other hand, the density of synapses might be massively underestimated, as the low frequency of spontaneous synaptic events may be due to the smaller surface area of NG2 cells when compared to that of neurons (Kukley et al., 2007; Kukley et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is presented as a possibility based on inference from cited studies about surface area and synaptic event frequency.

claim: The high-input impedance of thin dendritic branches could result in strong local depolarization even if the response arriving at the soma is small
source: Furthermore, the high-input impedance of the delicately thin dendritic branches could result in strong local depolarization even if the response arriving at the soma is small (Sun and Dietrich, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents an inference about electrical properties of dendrites.

claim: NG2 cells recorded in current-clamp mode showed a substantial peak depolarization of PSPs up to −35.4 ± 8.6 mV
source: In four NG2 cells resting at −85 mV, we recorded a substantial peak depolarization of PSPs up to −35.4 ± 8.6 mV (n=4, Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from current-clamp recordings shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Large mock PSPs are shortened when compared to small mock PSPs
source: Large mock PSPs (black lines) are shortened when compared to small mock PSPs (dashed lines, scaled for comparison).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C comparing mock PSP waveforms.

claim: 4-aminopyridine (4-AP) potently reversed the shortening of the mock PSP and significantly increased the half-width from 2.4 ± 0.2 ms to 3.8 ± 0.5 ms
source: The A-type K+-channel blocker 4-aminopyridine (4-AP) potently reversed the shortening of the mock PSP and significantly increased the half-width from 2.4 ± 0.2 ms to 3.8 ± 0.5 ms (n=4, Paired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from pharmacological manipulation with statistical testing.

claim: 4-AP increased the amplitude of the mock PSP from 65.8 ± 2.1 mV to 78.7 ± 4.3 mV
source: In addition, 4-AP increased the amplitude of the mock PSP from 65.8 ± 2.1 mV to 78.7 ± 4.3 mV (significantly different, s.d., Paired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical testing.

claim: Blocking Na+ channels by using tetrodotoxin (TTX) significantly reduced the amplitude from 66.1 ± 0.9 mV to 57.9 ± 1.1 mV
source: By contrast, blocking Na+ channels by using tetrodotoxin (TTX) significantly reduced the amplitude from 66.1 ± 0.9 mV to 57.9 ± 1.1 mV (n=7, Paired t-test)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from pharmacological manipulation with statistical testing.

claim: TTX slightly increased the half width of PSPs from 2.3 ± 0.3 ms to 3.0 ± 0.2 ms
source: and also slightly increased the half width of PSPs (from 2.3 ± 0.3 ms to 3.0 ± 0.2 ms, s.d., Paired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical testing.

claim: Delayed rectifier K+ channels are not recruited by individual mock PSPs because tetraethylammonium (TEA) affected neither their amplitude nor their half-width
source: Delayed rectifier K+ channels are not recruited by individual mock PSPs because tetraethylammonium (TEA) affected neither their amplitude nor their half-width (n = 6, Paired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from pharmacological manipulation with statistical testing.

claim: A-type channels shorten mock PSPs when NG2 cells are depolarized above −60 mV
source: A-type channels shorten mock PSPs when NG2 cells are depolarized above −60 mV.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Near the maximally attainable average depolarization of −16.5 ± 1.0 mV, the half-width ratio of mock PSPs was substantially shortened to 47.1 ± 3.4%
source: Near the maximally attainable average depolarization of −16.5 ± 1.0 mV, the half-width ratio of mock PSPs was substantially shortened to 47.1 ± 3.4% (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The shortening of mock PSPs is almost exclusively due to the action of A-type K+ channels
source: This shortening is almost exclusively due to the action of A-type K+ channels, whereas blocking Na+ and delayed-rectifier K+ channels did not detectably change the duration of mock PSPs (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing effects of different channel blockers shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: The amplitude of mock PSPs scales linearly with input strength in control conditions
source: In contrast to the half-width, the amplitude of mock PSPs was only slightly reduced, as indicated by an amplitude ratio near 1 even for large PSPs (Figure 2E, black line).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Linear scaling of the amplitude of mock PSPs in control conditions is a result of a balanced interplay of fast Na+ and A-type K+ channels
source: This linear scaling of the amplitude of mock PSPs in control conditions is a result of a balanced interplay of fast Na+ and A-type K+ channels (Figure 2C,E)
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing opposing effects of Na+ and K+ channel blockers.

claim: When A-type channels are blocked, the amplitude of mock PSPs is increased by ~15%
source: if A-type or Na+ channels are blocked, the amplitude of mock PSPs is increased or decreased by ~15% and ~30%, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from pharmacological manipulations.

claim: When Na+ channels are blocked, the amplitude of mock PSPs is decreased by ~30%
source: if A-type or Na+ channels are blocked, the amplitude of mock PSPs is increased or decreased by ~15% and ~30%, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from pharmacological manipulations.

claim: Synaptic activity induces rapid Ca2+ signals in NG2 cells mediated by low-voltage activated Ca2+ channels
source: Synaptic activity induces rapid Ca2+ signals mediated by low-voltage activated Ca2+ channels under strict inhibitory control of voltage-gated A-type K+ channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from calcium imaging combined with electrophysiology and pharmacology.

claim: Ca2+ signals in NG2 cells are under strict inhibitory control of voltage-gated A-type K+ channels
source: Synaptic activity induces rapid Ca2+ signals mediated by low-voltage activated Ca2+ channels under strict inhibitory control of voltage-gated A-type K+ channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing enhanced Ca2+ signals when A-type K+ channels are blocked.

claim: Mock PSP stimulation (10 mock PSPs at 100 Hz) triggered clear calcium transients in the soma and proximal dendrites (3.9 ± 1.3% and 12.7 ± 1.4%)
source: Indeed, we detected clear calcium transients in the soma and proximal dendrites (3.9 ± 1.3% and 12.7 ± 1.4%, Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from 2-photon calcium imaging shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Ca2+ signals in NG2 cells required the activation of VGCCs, as they were highly sensitive to a cocktail of VGCCs blockers
source: These Ca2+ signals required the activation of VGCCs, as they were highly sensitive to a cocktail of VGCCs blockers (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing blockade of Ca2+ signals by VGCC blockers shown in Figures 3F and 3G.

claim: Ca2+ signals in NG2 cells are mediated by low-voltage-activated Ca2+ channels, as shown by high sensitivity to combined application of SNX-482 and TTA-P2
source: Further, the high sensitivity of Ca2+ signals to combined application of SNX-482 (1 µM, R-type VGCCs blocker, Newcomb et al., 1998) and TTA-P2 (30 µM, T-type VGCCs blocker, Choe et al., 2011) suggested that they are mediated by low-voltage-activated Ca2+ channels (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from pharmacological manipulations shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: Na+/Ca2+ exchangers are not involved in mock EPSP-induced Ca2+ signals as blocking these exchangers with KB-R7943 did not decrease their amplitude
source: In contrast, Na+/Ca2+ exchangers, which were previously shown to mediate pharmacologically induced Ca2+ signals, are not involved in mock EPSP-induced Ca2+ signals as blocking these exchangers with KB-R7943 (10 µM, Iwamoto et al., 1996) did not decrease their amplitude (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from pharmacological manipulation shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: Ca2+ signals decayed back to baseline in an exponential manner with τdecay=3.16 ± 0.5 s
source: Ca2+ signals decayed back to baseline in an exponential manner (τdecay=3.16 ± 0.5 s, n=9, see Materials and methods, Figure 4C)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from calcium imaging analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Ca2+ signals could be reproducibly elicited over a period of more than 12 min
source: and could be reproducibly elicited over a period of more than 12 min (Figure 4D, n=5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from repeated calcium imaging shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Somatic current injection regularly produced a calcium response in proximal dendrites
source: Because somatic current injection regularly produced a calcium response in proximal dendrites, we analyzed the spatiotemporal distribution of calcium in NG2 cells in more detail by combining 2-photon microscopy and fast frame acquisition (30 Hz).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations from calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Injection of 10 mock PSPs generated an almost immediate increase in fluorescence throughout all scanned dendrites
source: Injection of 10 mock PSPs as above generated an almost immediate increase in fluorescence throughout all scanned dendrites, which decayed on the order of several seconds (Figure 5B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fast frame-scan calcium imaging shown in Figures 5B and 5D.

claim: The Ca2+ signal amplitude remained constant throughout the dendritic tree, or even increased towards the periphery
source: This analysis showed that the Ca2+ signal amplitude remained constant throughout the dendritic tree, or even increased towards the periphery (Figure 5D and E)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from spatial analysis of calcium signals shown in Figures 5D and 5E.

claim: The Ca2+ signal started almost simultaneously, irrespective of the distance from the soma
source: and that the signal started almost simultaneously, irrespective of the distance from the soma (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from temporal analysis of calcium signal onset shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The spread of the Ca2+ signal was much faster than expected from pure diffusional propagation from the soma into dendrites
source: In particular, the spread of the Ca2+ signal was much faster than expected from pure diffusional propagation from the soma into dendrites (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data to theoretical predictions shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The membrane depolarization of the mock PSPs rapidly spreads throughout the dendritic tree and opens local dendritic VGCCs
source: Together with the undiminished amplitude and steep rise of the dendritic Ca2+ signal, the data suggest that the membrane depolarization of the mock PSPs rapidly spreads throughout the dendritic tree and opens local dendritic VGCCs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from multiple experimental observations about calcium signal properties.

claim: The minimal delay and rapid rise of dendritic Ca2+ signals in NG2 cells is comparable to the fast dendritic Ca2+ responses of CA1 pyramidal neurons
source: The minimal delay and the rapid rise of dendritic Ca2+ signals in NG2 cells is comparable to the fast dendritic Ca2+ responses of CA1 pyramidal neurons recorded and stimulated under identical conditions (Figure 5G and H)
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative experimental data shown in Figures 5G and 5H.

claim: NG2 cells are capable of similar dendritic signal processing as CA1 pyramidal neurons
source: suggesting that NG2 cells are capable of similar dendritic signal processing.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of calcium signal kinetics between NG2 cells and neurons.

claim: When blocking A-type K+ channels with 4-AP, larger depolarizations often carrying prominent spikelets (in five out of seven cells, average amplitude 40.2 ± 6.7 mV) were observed, which were accompanied by substantial intracellular Ca2+ elevations
source: By contrast, when blocking A-type K+ channels, we observed larger depolarizations often carrying prominent spikelets (in five out of seven cells, average amplitude 40.2 ± 6.7 mV), which were accompanied by substantial intracellular Ca2+ elevations (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from pharmacological manipulation shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Ca2+ responses are much more frequent if NG2 cells are depolarized beyond approximately −45 mV
source: This analysis revealed (Figure 7A) that for both groups Ca2+ responses (filled symbols) are much more frequent if NG2 cells are depolarized beyond approximately −45 mV
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Ca2+ signals were significantly more frequent in the presence of 4-AP (control: 9/40; 4-AP: 22/43)
source: Ca2+ signals were not only significantly more frequent in the presence of 4-AP (control: 9/40; 4-AP: 22/43; Fisher's exact test, Figure 7B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical testing shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Responding trials showed a significantly larger Ca2+ signal amplitude in 4-AP (10.1 ± 0.7% control vs 14.1 ± 1.5% 4-AP)
source: but the responding trials also showed a significantly larger amplitude: 10.1 ± 0.7% and 14.1 ± 1.5% in the control and 4-AP groups, respectively (Student's t-test, Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical testing shown in Figure 7C.

claim: 4-AP treatment lowered the 50% threshold for Ca2+ responses from ~1200 to ~600 quanta
source: However, 4-AP treatment left-shifted this curve, lowered the 50% threshold from ~1200 to ~600 quanta, and thereby strongly increased the propensity of NG2 glial cells to generate Ca2+ signals (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Dendritic Ca2+ levels linearly increased with input strength when A-type K+ channels were blocked
source: This analysis revealed a small but statistically significant Ca2+ signal in the control group and also showed that dendritic Ca2+ levels linearly increased with input strength when A-type K+ channels were blocked (Figure 7F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: A-type K+ channels tightly gate the generation of Ca2+ signals in response to synaptic input to NG2 cells
source: In summary, these results indicate that A-type K+ channels tightly gate the generation of Ca2+ signals in response to synaptic input to NG2 cells.
evidence: This claim is a summary inference from multiple experimental observations about the effects of A-type K+ channel blockade.

claim: 2-photon-based MNI-glutamate uncaging produced uncaging EPSPs (uEPSPs) which compared well in amplitude and kinetics to the small spontaneously occurring fast EPSPs in NG2 cells
source: By pointing the scanner at segments in the outer two thirds of the NG2 cell dendritic tree (see scheme in Figure 8A, grey shaded area and Figure 8B), we produced uncaging EPSPs (uEPSPs, Figure 8C), which compared well in amplitude and kinetics to the small spontaneously occurring fast EPSPs in NG2 cells (Figure 8D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing uncaging-evoked and spontaneous EPSPs shown in Figures 8C, 8D, and 8E.

claim: Generating six uEPSPs within the same dendritic subsegment almost simultaneously produced a compound uEPSP with an amplitude of 3.2 ± 0.9 mV, whereas arithmetic summation of the six sequentially acquired responses amounted to 4.4 ± 1.3 mV
source: Generating six uEPSPs within the same dendritic subsegment almost simultaneously produced a compound uEPSP with an amplitude of 3.2 ± 0.9 mV, whereas arithmetic summation of the six sequentially acquired responses from the same individual positions amounted to 4.4 ± 1.3 mV (Figure 8C bottom panel, F, G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from glutamate uncaging experiments shown in Figures 8C, 8F, and 8G.

claim: Under control conditions, adding six uEPSPs to the mock PSP hardly increased the depolarization (−40.8 ± 1.4 mV vs −39.6 ± 1.3 mV)
source: Under control conditions, the addition of six uEPSPs to the mock PSP hardly increased the depolarization (−40.8 ± 1.4 mV vs −39.6 ± 1.3 mV, Figure 9B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from combined current injection and glutamate uncaging shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Under control conditions, adding six uEPSPs to mock PSP did not generate an increased calcium response in the stimulated dendrite (6.0 ± 1.2% vs 8.8 ± 2.5% ∆F/F)
source: and also did not generate an increased calcium response in the stimulated dendrite (6.0 ± 1.2% vs 8.8 ± 2.5% ∆F/F, one-way ANOVA for correlated samples, Tukey HSD, Figure 9B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical testing shown in Figures 9B and 9D.

claim: In the presence of 4-AP, adding local uEPSPs significantly boosted the Ca2+ signal in the stimulated dendrite (6.7 ± 1.3% vs 14.3 ± 3.3% ∆F/F)
source: However, adding local uEPSPs significantly boosted the Ca2+ signal in the stimulated dendrite (6.7 ± 1.3% vs 14.3 ± 3.3% ∆F/F, one-way ANOVA for correlated samples, Tukey HSD, Figure 9C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical testing shown in Figures 9C and 9D.

claim: Dendritic intracellular Ca2+ levels in NG2 cells indicate the activity of local synaptic input despite the small amplitude of the locally induced synaptic potential
source: Taken together, these data show that dendritic intracellular Ca2+ levels in NG2 cells indicate the activity of local synaptic input despite the small amplitude of the locally induced synaptic potential.
evidence: This claim is a summary inference from the glutamate uncaging experiments.

claim: The half-width of mock PSP voltage responses in a train (10 PSPs at 100 Hz) showed a clear increase of 26.3 ± 3.3%
source: When plotting the half-width of the mock PSP voltage responses in a train (10 PSPs at 100 Hz), we found a clear increase of 26.3 ± 3.3% (n=7, Figure 10A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from repetitive stimulation shown in Figures 10A and 10B.

claim: Progressive broadening of PSPs in a train is very likely to reflect an increasing fraction of inactivated A-type K+ channels as this broadening was not observed in the 4-AP-treated group
source: This progressive broadening of PSPs is very likely to reflect an increasing fraction of inactivated A-type K+ channels as this broadening was not observed in the 4-AP-treated group (n=8, Figure 10A,B).
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison of control and 4-AP treated groups shown in Figures 10A and 10B.

claim: With broadened PSPs in the 4-AP treated group, a significantly increased Ca2+ response was observed (12.7 ± 1.4% vs 24.2 ± 4.2% in the control and 4-AP groups, respectively)
source: Indeed, with broadened PSPs in the 4-AP treated group, we observed a significantly increased Ca2+ response (Figure 10C and D, 12.7 ± 1.4% vs 24.2 ± 4.2% in the control and 4-AP groups, respectively, Student's t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical testing shown in Figures 10C and 10D.

claim: Amplification of mock PSP-induced Ca2+ signals was also seen when voltage-gated K+ channels were blocked by the inclusion of Cs+ in the pipette solution (12.7 ± 1.4% vs 30.5 ± 9.3% in control and Cs+ groups, respectively)
source: Amplification of mock PSP-induced Ca2+ signals was also seen when voltage-gated K+ channels were blocked by the inclusion of Cs+ in the pipette solution (n = 10, Figure 10C and D, 12.7 ± 1.4% vs 30.5 ± 9.3% in control and Cs+ groups, respectively, Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical testing shown in Figures 10C and 10D.

claim: Ca2+ stores are not important for mock PSP-induced Ca2+ signals in NG2 cells
source: Furthermore, the pipette solution also contained 1 µM of the SERCA blocker thapsigargin and thus showed that Ca2+ stores are not important for mock PSP-induced Ca2+ signals in NG2 cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using thapsigargin to block Ca2+ stores.

claim: Synaptic transmitter release can trigger local Ca2+ signals in NG2 cell dendrites
source: Therefore, we designed an experiment to show that synaptic transmitter release can trigger local Ca2+ signals in NG2 cell dendrites.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from local synaptic stimulation shown in Figure 10E.

claim: Dendritically induced EPSPs (five or six stimuli at 100 HZ) were recorded with small amplitudes by the electrode attached to the soma (7.1 ± 1.1 mV)
source: As seen with local glutamate uncaging, these dendritically induced EPSPs were recorded with small amplitudes by the electrode attached to the soma (7.1 ± 1.1 mV, n=4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from local synaptic stimulation.

claim: Dendritically induced EPSPs were accompanied by a clear Ca2+ signal with kinetics and size similar to those induced by current injection or glutamate uncaging (21.1 ± 3.4%)
source: Nevertheless, in the nearby dendrite, these EPSPs were accompanied by a clear Ca2+ signal with kinetics and size similar to those shown above for Ca2+ signals induced by current injection or glutamate uncaging (21.1 ± 3.4%, n=4, Figure 10E, 1 µM thapsigargin in the pipette).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from local synaptic stimulation shown in Figure 10E.

claim: The local depolarization in the dendrite is much larger than that observed at the soma and there is strong voltage attenuation along a dendrite
source: Furthermore, as argued above, this observation also suggested that the local depolarization in the dendrite is much larger than that observed at the soma and that there is strong voltage attenuation along a dendrite.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of large dendritic Ca2+ signals despite small somatic voltage responses.

claim: NG2 cells are effective integrators of synaptic activity
source: The key finding of the present study is that NG2 cells, which were previously believed to be electrically unexcitable, are effective integrators of synaptic activity.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the main findings from all experiments in the study.

claim: NG2 cells possess two elaborate integration modes governed by A-type K+ channels: local compartmentalized integration in individual dendritic subunits, versus global integration leading to massive Ca2+ influx throughout the entire dendritic arborization
source: Moreover, they possess two elaborate integration modes governed by A-type K+ channels: local compartmentalized integration in individual dendritic subunits, versus global integration leading to massive Ca2+ influx throughout the entire dendritic arborization of NG2 cells.
evidence: This claim is a summary inference from multiple experimental observations about local and global Ca2+ signals.

claim: NG2 cells use Ca2+ levels to gradually encode the level of synaptic activity itself
source: Thus, in contrast to neurons, NG2 cells use Ca2+ levels to gradually encode the level of synaptic activity itself.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Ca2+ signal amplitude scales with input strength.

claim: Ca2+ signals in NG2 cells decay with a time constant on the order of seconds, while the Ca2+ levels in neurons usually return to baseline within several hundred milliseconds
source: Both locally induced and global Ca2+ signals in NG2 cells decay with a time constant on the order of seconds, while the Ca2+ levels in neurons usually return to baseline within several hundred milliseconds.
evidence: This claim combines experimental data from NG2 cells with established knowledge about neuronal Ca2+ signals.

claim: The low incremental amplitude, slow return to baseline, and reliable occurrence even in distal dendrites make Ca2+ signals in NG2 cells effective for integrating synaptic input of a wide range of frequencies across their dendritic tree
source: Their low incremental amplitude, their slow return to baseline, and their reliable occurrence even in distal dendrites are characteristics displayed by Ca2+ signals in NG2 cells that are key to effectively integrating synaptic input of a wide range of frequencies across their dendritic tree.
evidence: This claim is an inference about functional significance based on the observed properties of Ca2+ signals.

claim: Voltage-gated channels are found in thin dendrites which act as compartmentalized processing units and generate local calcium transients
source: However, voltage-gated channels are also found in thin dendrites which act as compartmentalized processing units and generate local calcium transients.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing local dendritic Ca2+ signals and is inferred from the properties of these signals.

claim: The activity-dependent control of Ca2+ signals by A-type channels and the global versus local signaling domains make intracellular Ca2+ in NG2 cells a prime signaling molecule to transform neurotransmitter release into activity-dependent myelination
source: Taken together, the activity-dependent control of Ca2+ signals by A-type channels and the global versus local signaling domains make intracellular Ca2+ in NG2 cells a prime signaling molecule to transform neurotransmitter release into activity-dependent myelination.
evidence: This claim is a speculative conclusion about the functional significance of the findings for myelination.

claim: NG2 cells perform linear integration of glutamatergic synaptic inputs and respond with increasing dendritic calcium elevations
source: Here we show that NG2 cells perform linear integration of glutamatergic synaptic inputs and respond with increasing dendritic calcium elevations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing linear scaling of Ca2+ signals with input strength.

claim: Ca2+ signals can be global and originate throughout the cell
source: Ca2+ signals can be global and originate throughout the cell.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from frame-scan imaging showing simultaneous Ca2+ signals throughout the dendritic tree.

claim: NG2 cells possess a dedicated signal integration machinery, different from that of neurons and other types of glial cells
source: We report that NG2 cells possess a dedicated signal integration machinery, different from that of neurons and other types of glial cells, and generate local dendritic or global Ca2+ responses depending on the pattern and type of incoming activity.
evidence: This claim is a summary inference from all experimental findings comparing NG2 cells to neurons and other glia.

claim: NG2 cells generate local dendritic or global Ca2+ responses depending on the pattern and type of incoming activity
source: We report that NG2 cells possess a dedicated signal integration machinery, different from that of neurons and other types of glial cells, and generate local dendritic or global Ca2+ responses depending on the pattern and type of incoming activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing both local and global Ca2+ signals under different stimulation conditions.

claim: Post-natal 7–15-day old transgenic mice expressing DsRed fluorescent protein under control of the promoter of mouse Cspg4 gene were used in this study
source: Post-natal 7–15-day old (male and female) transgenic mice expressing DsRed fluorescent protein under control of the promoter of mouse Cspg4 gene were used in this study (NG2-DsRed transgenic mouse line [Zhu et al., 2008]).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the experimental model used.

claim: A total of 12 recorded DsRed+ cells were tested and verified to be NG2 positive
source: A total of 12 recorded DsRed+ cells were tested and verified to be NG2 positive.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical verification data.

claim: The average input resistance of all NG2 cells included in the study was 251.4 ± 18.4 MΩ
source: The average input resistance of all NG2 cells included in the study was 251.4 ± 18.4 MΩ (n=132, range 37 to 1483 MΩ).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements.

claim: The average resting potential was −83.8 ± 0.7 mV
source: The average resting potential (no current injection) was −83.8 ± 0.7 mV (n=132).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements.

claim: Brief trains of action potentials (50–100 ms) should be very effective at inactivating A-type channels and will open the 'calcium-gate' in NG2 cells
source: Based on previous reports on the kinetics of A-type K+ channels (Steinhauser et al., 1994b), our data allows us to predict that brief trains of action potentials (50–100 ms) should be very effective at inactivating A-type channels and will open the 'calcium-gate' in NG2 cells.
evidence: This claim is a prediction based on experimental data and cited literature about A-type channel kinetics.

claim: There is evidence for developmental and reactive regulation of K+ channels in response to ischemia/injury
source: Indeed, there is evidence for developmental and reactive regulation of K+ channels in response to ischemia/injury (Lytle et al., 2009; Pivonkova et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Synaptically induced Ca2+ signaling is well-suited to initiate actions of NG2 cells in the context of activity-dependent myelination
source: Based on our present findings, we propose that synaptically induced Ca2+ signaling is well-suited to initiate actions of NG2 cells in the context of activity-dependent myelination.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about the functional significance of the findings.

claim: Local Ca2+ signals could be involved in stabilizing or enhancing contact sites with individual axons
source: Such local Ca2+ signals could be involved in stabilizing or enhancing contact sites with individual axons (Hines et al., 2015; Mensch et al., 2015) and could enable axon-specific integration and computation.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the function of local Ca2+ signals, supported by citations.

claim: Global Ca2+ signals are particularly qualified for triggering global cellular actions, such as division, differentiation, survival or motility of NG2 cells in response to neuronal activity
source: On the other hand, global Ca2+ signals, which are induced by a larger number of active synapses throughout the dendritic tree, spread within the NG2 cell and involve the soma, are particularly qualified for triggering global cellular actions, such as division, differentiation, survival or motility of NG2 cells in response to neuronal activity.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the function of global Ca2+ signals based on their properties.

claim: NG2 cells possess a dedicated synaptic integration repertoire, distinct from that of neurons and other types of glial cells, by encoding the number of active synapses in a graded fashion
source: In conclusion, our study shows for the first time that NG2 cells possess a dedicated synaptic integration repertoire, distinct from that of neurons and other types of glial cells, by encoding the number of active synapses in a graded fashion.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on all experimental findings.

claim: This integration builds on Ca2+ signals in different spatial domains and appears as a specialized type of Ca2+ excitability of NG2 cells
source: This integration builds on Ca2+ signals in different spatial domains and appears as a specialized type of Ca2+ excitability of NG2 cells.
evidence: This is a summary inference about the mechanism of integration based on experimental findings.

claim: Voltage-gated K+ channels dampen Ca2+ signals but this can be overcome by temporally and spatially coincident synaptic depolarizations
source: Voltage-gated K+ channels dampen Ca2+ signals but this can be overcome by temporally and spatially coincident synaptic depolarizations.
evidence: This is a summary inference from experimental data showing the effects of K+ channels and their inactivation.

claim: Specific patterns of axonal activity may promote myelination by instructing NG2 cells to interact with axons or generate new oligodendrocytes
source: Thus, specific patterns of axonal activity may promote myelination by instructing NG2 cells to interact with axons or generate new oligodendrocytes.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about the functional implications of the findings for myelination.
